cards.back: To gather or collect something over time, gradually increasing in quantity. Example: 'Students who accumulate knowledge through consistent study tend to perform better on standardized exams.'
To accept or recognize the existence, truth, or validity of something. Example: 'The researchers acknowledged the limitations of their study in the final section of the paper.'
To adjust or modify oneself or something to suit new conditions or circumstances. Example: 'Immigrants often need time to adapt to the cultural norms of their new country.'
Sufficient or acceptable in quality or quantity for a particular purpose. Example: 'The hospital lacked adequate funding to upgrade its outdated medical equipment.'
To publicly recommend or support a particular cause, policy, or action. Example: 'Many environmental groups advocate the use of renewable energy sources to combat climate change.'
To distribute resources or duties for a particular purpose. Example: 'The university allocated additional funds to scientific research programs.'
To change or modify something, usually in a relatively small but significant way. Example: 'The government decided to alter its immigration policy in response to public concern.'
Open to more than one interpretation; not having a single clear meaning. Example: 'The survey questions were too ambiguous, which led to unreliable results.'
A comparison between two things for the purpose of explanation or clarification. Example: 'The professor drew an analogy between the human brain and a computer to explain information processing.'
To expect or predict something and prepare for it in advance. Example: 'Urban planners must anticipate population growth when designing new infrastructure.'
Clearly visible or understood; obvious. Example: 'The apparent decline in reading habits among young people has prompted educational reforms.'
Close to the actual value or figure but not completely exact. Example: 'The approximate cost of the construction project was estimated at twelve million dollars.'
Based on random choice or personal whim rather than any reason or system. Example: 'Critics argued that the selection criteria appeared arbitrary and lacked transparency.'
A particular part, feature, or element of something. Example: 'One important aspect of language learning is regular exposure to native speakers.'
To evaluate or estimate the nature, quality, or ability of something. Example: 'Teachers use a variety of methods to assess student performance throughout the semester.'
To regard something as being caused by a particular factor. Example: 'Researchers attribute the rise in obesity to sedentary lifestyles and poor dietary choices.'
The mass or majority of something; a large quantity. Example: 'The bulk of government spending is directed toward healthcare and education.'
The maximum amount that something can contain, produce, or handle. Example: 'The new stadium has the capacity to hold over fifty thousand spectators.'
To come to an end or to bring something to an end. Example: 'The factory was ordered to cease operations until environmental standards were met.'
To direct something toward a particular end or purpose. Example: 'The organization channels its resources into community development projects.'
To refer to a source of information as evidence or justification. Example: 'In academic writing, it is essential to cite all sources to avoid plagiarism.'
To make a statement or situation less confused and more understandable. Example: 'The lecturer paused to clarify the distinction between correlation and causation.'
To occur at the same time or correspond in position or nature. Example: 'The rise in housing prices coincided with a period of rapid economic growth.'
To fall down or give way suddenly; to fail completely. Example: 'Several financial institutions collapsed during the global economic crisis of 2008.'
To begin or start something, especially formally. Example: 'Construction of the new library is expected to commence in early spring.'
A raw material or primary agricultural product that can be bought and sold. Example: 'Oil remains one of the most traded commodities in the global market.'
To collect and assemble information from various sources into a single document or list. Example: 'The research team compiled data from over two hundred interviews for the study.'
To add to something in a way that enhances or improves it. Example: 'Practical laboratory sessions complement the theoretical knowledge gained in lectures.'
A part or element of a larger whole. Example: 'Critical thinking is a key component of academic success at the university level.'
Including or dealing with all or nearly all elements or aspects of something. Example: 'The report provides a comprehensive analysis of the factors contributing to urban pollution.'
To form or devise an idea or plan in the mind. Example: 'The architect conceived an innovative design that blended modern and traditional elements.'
Existing, happening, or done at the same time. Example: 'The university offers concurrent enrollment in both undergraduate and graduate courses.'
To keep or restrict someone or something within certain limits. Example: 'The discussion was confined to issues directly related to public health policy.'
To comply with rules, standards, or expectations. Example: 'All submitted essays must conform to the formatting guidelines specified in the handbook.'
Permission or agreement for something to happen. Example: 'Participants in the study were required to give written consent before any data was collected.'
Notably large in size, amount, or extent. Example: 'The project required a considerable investment of both time and financial resources.'
To be a part of a whole; to make up or form something. Example: 'Women now constitute nearly half of the total workforce in many developed nations.'
To severely restrict the scope, extent, or activity of something. Example: 'Budget cuts constrained the department from hiring additional research staff.'
Belonging to or occurring in the present time. Example: 'Contemporary architecture often prioritizes sustainability and energy efficiency.'
To deny the truth of a statement by asserting the opposite. Example: 'The new findings contradict earlier assumptions about the effectiveness of the treatment.'
Prolonged public disagreement or heated discussion about a subject. Example: 'The proposed education reform sparked considerable controversy among teachers and parents.'
To change the form, character, or function of something. Example: 'Several old warehouses have been converted into modern apartment complexes.'
To work jointly with others toward a shared goal. Example: 'Nations must cooperate to address global challenges such as climate change and poverty.'
To organize different elements or people so they work together effectively. Example: 'The relief agency coordinated efforts among multiple organizations to deliver aid efficiently.'
To have a close similarity or connection; to match or be equivalent. Example: 'The results of the experiment correspond closely to the predictions made by the theoretical model.'
Of great importance; decisive or critical. Example: 'Access to clean water is crucial for preventing the spread of waterborne diseases.'
A system of money in general use in a particular country. Example: 'Fluctuations in currency exchange rates can significantly affect international trade.'
To arrive at a conclusion by reasoning from available evidence or premises. Example: 'From the data presented, one can deduce that exercise has a positive effect on mental health.'
To clearly show the existence or truth of something by giving proof or evidence. Example: 'The experiment demonstrated that plants grow faster under blue light than red light.'
To be a sign of; to indicate or represent. Example: 'In the chart, the darker shading denotes regions with higher population density.'
To obtain something from a particular source or origin. Example: 'Many English words are derived from Latin and Greek roots.'
To discover or identify the presence or existence of something. Example: 'Advanced sensors can detect pollutants in water at extremely low concentrations.'
To depart from an established course, standard, or norm. Example: 'The actual results deviated significantly from what the researchers had predicted.'
To give time, attention, or resources entirely to a particular activity or cause. Example: 'She devoted three years of research to understanding the effects of urbanization on wildlife.'
To recognize or identify what makes something distinct from others. Example: 'It is important to differentiate between facts and opinions when evaluating media sources.'
To make or become less in size, importance, or value. Example: 'The influence of traditional media has diminished with the rise of social networking platforms.'
Individually separate and distinct from others. Example: 'The research identified three discrete stages in the development of language skills in children.'
To move something or someone from its usual or proper place. Example: 'Natural disasters displaced thousands of families from their homes last year.'
Recognizably different in nature from something else; clearly separate. Example: 'The study identified two distinct patterns of consumer behavior in urban and rural areas.'
To give a misleading or false account or impression of something. Example: 'Media coverage can sometimes distort public perception of scientific findings.'
Showing a great deal of variety; very different from each other. Example: 'A diverse workforce brings a wider range of perspectives and ideas to an organization.'
Relating to the internal affairs of a country; occurring within one's own country. Example: 'Domestic tourism has grown as more people choose to explore destinations within their own borders.'
To have a commanding influence or control over something. Example: 'A small number of multinational corporations dominate the global technology market.'
To completely remove or get rid of something. Example: 'The new filtration system was designed to eliminate harmful bacteria from the water supply.'
Based on observation or experience rather than theory or pure logic. Example: 'The hypothesis must be supported by empirical evidence before it can be widely accepted.'
To intensify, increase, or further improve the quality or value of something. Example: 'Interactive digital tools can enhance the learning experience for students of all ages.'
To gradually wear away or diminish over time. Example: 'Public trust in the institution has eroded due to a series of financial scandals.'
Clearly seen or understood; obvious. Example: 'It is evident from the survey data that public attitudes toward recycling have shifted significantly.'
To develop gradually over time, especially from a simple to a more complex form. Example: 'Educational methods have evolved considerably with the introduction of digital technology.'
To go beyond what is allowed, expected, or thought possible. Example: 'The company's annual revenue exceeded initial projections by nearly twenty percent.'
To display or show a quality, behavior, or characteristic. Example: 'Children raised in bilingual households often exhibit greater cognitive flexibility.'
Stated clearly and in detail, leaving no room for confusion or doubt. Example: 'The assignment instructions were explicit about the required referencing style.'
To make a process or action easier or more achievable. Example: 'Online platforms facilitate communication between students and instructors outside of class hours.'
To rise and fall irregularly in number or amount. Example: 'Oil prices tend to fluctuate in response to geopolitical events and changes in supply.'
A basic structure underlying a system, concept, or text. Example: 'The researchers developed a theoretical framework to guide their investigation into social inequality.'
